# Volume 1 — CHAPTER I. Mrs. Agatha Sowerby Is Surprised

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

MRS. Agatha Sowerby’s home was situated exactly where the principal road in Brierley sloped down into a small ravine, bordered with alders and ladies’ eardrops and crossed by a rivulet whose origin lay far behind in the forest of the old Abernethy place; that rivulet was said to be a complex, rushing stream in its initial path through that forest, possessing murky secrets of deep water and waterfalls; however, once it arrived at Sowerby’s Hollow it had become a calm, properly behaved small watercourse, because no stream whatsoever could flow by Mrs. Agatha Sowerby’s house without showing proper respect for propriety and order; it likely realized that Mrs. Agatha sat by her window, maintaining a vigilant watch over every single passing thing, starting with streams and children on up, and that should she observe any strange or improper occurrence she would not settle until she had uncovered its underlying reasons.
{: #nw-v01-c01-p0000 }

A great many individuals, both inside Brierley and beyond, are able to pay strict attention to the affairs of their neighbors by virtue of ignoring their own; Mrs. Agatha Sowerby, however, belonged to that category of proficient women who are able to handle their personal affairs while simultaneously directing those of everyone else. Being an outstanding homemaker, her chores were perpetually finished and thoroughly executed; she directed the Sewing Circle, assisted in directing the Sunday-school, and served as the primary pillar of both the Church Aid Society and the Foreign Missions Auxiliary. Despite all these responsibilities, Mrs. Agatha discovered plenty of leisure to remain seated for hours beside her kitchen window, producing “cotton warp” quilts with her knitting needles—she had completed sixteen such items, a detail Brierley homemakers were accustomed to sharing in hushed, respectful tones—and maintaining a vigilant watch over the principal thoroughfare that traversed the valley and climbed the sharp red incline past it. Because Brierley was situated upon a tiny triangular strip of land projecting into the Gulf of St. Lawrence, surrounded by water on two sides, anyone entering or leaving the community was required to travel along that hillside path and thereby navigate the invisible scrutiny of Mrs. Agatha’s perceptive gaze.
{: #nw-v01-c01-p0001 }

During a single afternoon in the beginning of June, she was seated in that spot. Through the window, the sunshine entered with bright warmth, while a vast swarm of bees buzzed above the orchard on the slope beneath the home, which blushed like a bride in pinkish-white blossoms. Over on the hill field past the barn, Thomas Sowerby—a quiet, small man referred to by Brierley locals as “Agatha Sowerby’s husband”—was putting his late turnip seed into the ground; meanwhile, across by Grey Shutters on the large, red brook field, Obed Abernethy should have been putting in his own. Because she had overheard him telling Peter Morrison at William J. Blair’s shop in Delford the prior evening that he intended to plant his turnip seed the following afternoon, Mrs. Agatha was aware that he should be doing so. Naturally, Peter had been the one to inquire, since Obed Abernethy had not once in his entire existence offered details on any subject of his own accord.
{: #nw-v01-c01-p0002 }

Still, Obed Abernethy could be seen right here at three-thirty on a bustling afternoon, calmly traveling across the hollow and climbing the hill; furthermore, he was dressed in a white collar alongside his finest suit of clothes, clear evidence that his destination lay outside of Brierley; additionally, he was using the buggy paired with the sorrel mare, indicating a trip of significant length. So, what was Obed Abernethy's destination, and what reason did he have for traveling there?
{: #nw-v01-c01-p0003 }

If it had concerned any other person in Brierley, Mrs. Agatha, cleverly piecing things together, could have guessed both answers fairly well. However, because Obed left his house so seldom, his departure had to be driven by an urgent and extraordinary matter; he was the most timid person in existence and despised being surrounded by unfamiliar people or visiting anywhere he might need to converse. Obed, wearing fancy clothes with a white collar and riding in a buggy, was an uncommon occurrence. Mrs. Agatha, no matter how much she reflected on it, was unable to understand it, and the pleasure of her afternoon was ruined.
{: #nw-v01-c01-p0004 }

“Following tea, I will simply pop over to Grey Shutters and ascertain from Thirza his destination and reasoning,” the respectable woman ultimately decided. “Typically, he avoids traveling to town during this season and he avoids visiting entirely; had he exhausted his supply of turnip seed, he would not put on fine clothes and use the buggy for a replenishment; his driving speed was too slow for a medical errand. Nevertheless, some occurrence must have transpired since yesterday evening to cause his departure. I am utterly bewildered, indeed, and I shall not experience a single moment of mental or moral tranquility until I discover the reason for Obed Abernethy leaving Brierley this very day.”
{: #nw-v01-c01-p0005 }

Therefore, Mrs. Agatha departed following tea; her journey was short; a mere quarter of a mile up the road from Sowerby’s Hollow stood the large, sprawling house, surrounded by orchards, in which the Abernethys resided. Indeed, the distance was lengthened considerably by the long lane. When establishing his farmstead, Obed Abernethy’s father, who was just as bashful and quiet as his son would be later on, had distanced himself from other people as much as he could without genuinely withdrawing into the forest. Grey Shutters had been constructed on the outermost border of his cleared property, and it remained in that spot present day, hardly noticeable from the primary thoroughfare where every other Brierley house was positioned so companionably. Residing in a location like that was not considered real living by Mrs. Agatha Sowerby.
{: #nw-v01-c01-p0006 }

“It’s simply remaining, that is all,” she declared while walking down the deeply rutted, grass-covered path flanked by wild rose shrubs. “Living far back here alone, it is small surprise that Obed and Thirza are each somewhat strange. Trees do not provide much fellowship, even if, goodness knows, there would be plenty of them if they did. I would prefer to observe human beings. Certainly, they appear happy enough; yet then, I imagine, it is familiar to them. One can become accustomed to any situation, even to hanging, just as the Irishman remarked.”
{: #nw-v01-c01-p0007 }

Following this, Mrs. Agatha exited the lane and walked into the backyard belonging to Grey Shutters. Exceptionally green, tidy, and orderly was the yard, bounded along one edge by enormous patriarchal willows and along the opposite side by stiff Lombardies. Neither a stray stone nor stick could be spotted, because Mrs. Agatha would certainly have noticed it had one been present. In secret, she held the view that Thirza Abernethy swept the yard just as frequently as she swept her dwelling. A person could have consumed a meal directly from the earth without exceeding the proverbial peck of dirt.
{: #nw-v01-c01-p0008 }

Knocking sharply on the kitchen door, Mrs. Agatha entered after receiving permission. At Grey Shutters, the kitchen was a bright room—or it might have been bright had its extreme, agonizing cleanliness not imparted the look of an unoccupied parlor. Its windows faced east and west; through the western window, which overlooked the back yard, a wave of soft June sunshine poured; however, the eastern window, from which a person could catch sight of the flowering white cherry-trees in the left orchard and swaying, delicate birches down in the hollow beside the brook, was covered in green by a mass of vines. In this spot sat Thirza Abernethy, whenever she sat down, continuously somewhat suspicious of sunlight, a phenomenon she considered overly lively and flighty for a world designed for serious contemplation; and in this spot she sat currently, knitting, while the table positioned behind her was set for supper.
{: #nw-v01-c01-p0009 }

Even before the door was fully shut, Mrs. Agatha had registered mentally all that sat upon the table. The presence of three laid plates indicated that Thirza had to be awaiting somebody arriving with Obed for tea; however, the crockery was just the ordinary set and the spread contained merely crab-apple preserves alongside a single cake variety, meaning the anticipated guest could hardly be important. Still, how were Obed’s white collar and the sorrel mare to be explained? Mrs. Agatha found herself becoming quite lightheaded from this strange puzzle surrounding tranquil, unpuzzling Grey Shutters.
{: #nw-v01-c01-p0010 }

“Good evening, Agatha,” said Thirza briskly. “It’s a truly fine evening, isn’t it? Won’t you take a seat? How is everyone in your family?”
{: #nw-v01-c01-p0011 }

A bond which could only be termed friendship, for want of a better word, was present and had constantly been present between Thirza Abernethy and Mrs. Agatha, regardless of—or possibly owing to—how different they were.
{: #nw-v01-c01-p0012 }

With a tall, slender frame that had sharp angles rather than curves, Thirza possessed dark hair with graying strands that she constantly bound at the back in a tight, firm bun, pierced combatively by a pair of wire hairpins. She gave the impression of a person possessing a limited background and an unyielding sense of morality, attributes she indeed had; yet around her mouth lay a redeeming quality that, had it been nurtured just a bit more, could have been seen as a sign of a humorous disposition.
{: #nw-v01-c01-p0013 }

“We’re doing well enough,” Mrs. Agatha remarked. “However, I had a bit of a scare that you might not be, seeing Obed head out earlier today. My thought was that perhaps he was heading to the doctor’s office.”
{: #nw-v01-c01-p0014 }

A knowing twitch touched Thirza’s lips. Mrs. Agatha’s arrival was anticipated by her, as she realized that her neighbor’s inquisitiveness could not withstand the spectacle of Obed setting out so unexpectedly.
{: #nw-v01-c01-p0015 }

“Oh, no, I am completely fine, even though my head ached terribly yesterday,” she stated. “Obed travelled to Alder River. An orphan asylum located in Nova Scotia is sending us a young boy, who arrives on the train this evening.”
{: #nw-v01-c01-p0016 }

Had Thirza stated that Obed had travelled to Alder River for a meeting with a kangaroo originating from Australia, Mrs. Agatha’s level of surprise would have been no greater. For a full five seconds, she was quite literally rendered speechless. Although it defied belief that Thirza was mocking her, Mrs. Agatha found herself nearly compelled to believe just that.
{: #nw-v01-c01-p0017 }

“Are you in earnest, Thirza?” she demanded as soon as she recovered her voice.
{: #nw-v01-c01-p0018 }

“Certainly, indeed,” Thirza replied, treating the acquisition of young males from Nova Scotian orphanages as a routine springtime task on a properly managed Brierley farm, rather than an unprecedented novelty.
{: #nw-v01-c01-p0019 }

It seemed to Mrs. Agatha that a harsh shock had been delivered to her mind. Exclamation marks filled her thoughts. A male child! That Thirza and Obed Abernethy, out of everyone, had taken in a boy! Out of an orphanage! Truly, the earth was flipping on its head! From now on, no occurrence could astonish her! None at all!
{: #nw-v01-c01-p0020 }

“Whatever caused you to entertain an idea like that?” she inquired with clear disapproval.
{: #nw-v01-c01-p0021 }

Because her opinion was not requested before this was carried out, it inevitably required her condemnation.
{: #nw-v01-c01-p0022 }

“Well, we’ve been pondering it for a while—throughout the whole winter, actually,” Thirza replied. “Mrs. Alexander Tranter came up here one day prior to Christmas and mentioned her plan to obtain a young girl from the Marden asylum in the spring. Because her cousin resides there, Mrs. Tranter has paid her visits and understands everything about the place. Consequently, Obed and I have discussed the matter intermittently since then. We figured we would obtain a boy. Obed is advancing in age, as you know—he has reached sixty—and he lacks his former agility. His heart causes him significant trouble. Furthermore, you are aware of how extremely difficult securing hired labor has become. No one can ever be hired except those foolish, partially grown young French boys; and the moment you successfully train one to your routine and teach him something, he leaves abruptly for the States or the lobster canneries. Initially, Obed proposed acquiring a Home boy. However, I gave a firm ‘no’ to that idea. ‘They might be perfectly fine—I am not claiming otherwise—but I will not take any London street Arabs,’ I stated. ‘At minimum, provide me with someone native born. A risk will exist, regardless of whom we obtain. Nevertheless, my mind will be more at ease and my night’s sleep will be sounder if we obtain a born Canadian.’ Thus, we ultimately resolved to request that Mrs. Tranter select one for us when she traveled across to retrieve her young girl. Learning last week that she was departing, we dispatched word to her through Richard Tranter’s family at Delford to fetch us an intelligent, promising boy around ten or eleven years old. We concluded that age would be optimal—sufficiently old to assist with chores immediately and sufficiently young to be raised correctly. Our intention is to provide him with schooling and a comfortable home. Today we received a telegram from Mrs. Alexander Tranter—delivered from the station by the mail-man—announcing their arrival on the five-thirty train this evening. Therefore, Obed departed for Alder River to meet him. Mrs. Tranter intends to leave him there. Naturally, she continues onward to Pale Sands station herself.”
{: #nw-v01-c01-p0023 }

Mrs. Agatha was proud of her habit of always expressing her thoughts freely; after adapting her mindset to this astonishing bit of information, she went on to express them now.
{: #nw-v01-c01-p0024 }

“Well, Thirza, I’m simply going to state plainly that I believe you are doing an extremely silly thing—a hazardous thing, that is what. You have no idea what you are receiving. A unfamiliar child is being brought into your house and home by you, and you are completely ignorant about him, his temperament, the kind of parents he possessed, or the manner in which he is apt to develop. Why, just last week I came across a report in the newspaper regarding a husband and wife up west of the Island who received a boy from an orphan asylum, and during the night he ignited the house—ignited it intentionally, Thirza—and almost scorched them to a crisp inside their beds. Furthermore, I am aware of a different instance in which a foster boy habitually sucked the eggs—no one was able to cure him of the habit. Had you sought my counsel regarding this situation—which you omitted to do, Thirza—I would have advised you for goodness’ sake to refrain from considering such a notion, that is what.”
{: #nw-v01-c01-p0025 }

Thirza appeared neither alarmed nor offended by this comforting from Job. Her knitting continued steadily.
{: #nw-v01-c01-p0026 }

“I admit there is truth in your words, Agatha. I have felt some doubts of my own. However, Obed was exceedingly determined about it. Seeing that, I yielded. Obed so rarely fixes his heart on something that whenever he does, I constantly consider it my obligation to yield. Regarding the danger, danger exists in almost every action a person takes in life. There is danger when people bear their own offspring, for that matter—they do not always turn out properly. Furthermore, Nova Scotia is very near the Island. It is not as though we were obtaining him from England or the States. He cannot be very unlike us.”
{: #nw-v01-c01-p0027 }

“Well, my wish is for everything to work out fine,” stated Mrs. Agatha, her voice clearly showing her distressing misgivings. “Just refrain from claiming you were not cautioned by me should Grey Shutters be reduced to ashes by him or if he poisons the well using strychnine—a situation in New Brunswick came to my attention where a youth from an orphan home performed that very act, causing the entire household to perish in excruciating torment. Mind you, a girl was involved in that case.”
{: #nw-v01-c01-p0028 }

“Well, we aren’t obtaining a girl,” Thirza said, as though the contamination of wells was an exclusively female feat and not something to fear regarding a boy. “Taking a girl to raise is something I would not ever contemplate. Mrs. Alexander Tranter adopting one makes me wonder. Then again, she would not hesitate to adopt an entire asylum of orphans if the notion entered her mind.”
{: #nw-v01-c01-p0029 }

Mrs. Agatha would have preferred remaining until Obed arrived back with his imported orphan. However, considering that his return was still a full two hours away at minimum, she decided she would walk up the road to Robert Bell’s to share the information. Creating a stir that was surpassed by no other was something Mrs. Agatha truly enjoyed, and this would undoubtedly accomplish that. Therefore, she departed, which brought a degree of comfort to Thirza, whose misgivings and anxieties were beginning to resurface because of Mrs. Agatha’s negative outlook.
{: #nw-v01-c01-p0030 }

“Well, of all the events that have occurred or ever shall occur!” Mrs. Agatha exclaimed once she had safely reached the lane. “I truly feel like this has to be a dream. Well, without a doubt, my sympathies go out to that unfortunate young boy. Obed and Thirza lack any understanding of children, and they will demand that he possess more wisdom and composure than his very own grandfather, provided he ever possessed one, which remains uncertain. Somehow, imagining a youngster at Grey Shutters feels unnatural; no child has ever resided there, since Obed and Thirza had reached adulthood by the time the new home was constructed—assuming they were ever young themselves, an idea that is difficult to credit upon viewing them. Nothing could tempt me to step into that orphan's place. My goodness, I simply feel sorry for him, and that is the truth.”
{: #nw-v01-c01-p0031 }

Thus spoke Mrs. Agatha to the wild rose bushes from the depth of her emotions; yet had she been able to behold the youngster who was waiting patiently at the Alder River station at that exact instant, her compassion would have been even greater and more intense.
{: #nw-v01-c01-p0032 }
